transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-16 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya, Ethan, Sara (Redwood) — Priya, Liam, Jordan, Olivia (Hyacinth)

Summary:
High-level intake to understand Hyacinth's per-token burn sensitivity and which hosting path (hosted, dedicated, private/VPC) makes sense. Customer wants strict monthly budget cap, 99th pct latency targets for real-time chat (under 200ms ideally), and strong audit/KMS needs for CDR retention. Discussed batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization trade-offs and pilot scope.

Topics:
- current stack & traffic profile
- budget ceiling and success criteria
- latency SLAs and SLO targets
- tradeoffs: batching vs single-token latency, cache hit rates
- hosting options and residency/KMS requirements
- pilot definition and next steps

Action items: (captured above)

Transcript body (timestamps approx every 30–60s):
00:00 Maya (Redwood): okay everyone on the call? can you hear me?
00:05 Priya (Hyacinth): yeah we can, hey thanks for doing this. we've been trying to figure out the per-token budget for our new virtual assistant product so we're hoping to map hosting options to our monthly cap.
00:18 Ethan (Redwood SE): awesome. quick intro from our side — i'm ethan, i'll run through some performance knobs and how those change unit economics. maya will handle commercial and pilot next steps.
00:29 Liam (Hyacinth): quick context: we have around 3M user-facing messages per month today, spike to 10M in promos. real-time chat path is ~20% of messages but is the highest latency SLO. currently routing to an in-house microservice that calls an open model on rented GPUs. burn is high and ops cost is spiking.
00:49 Maya: got it. and what's your target latency and monthly budget?
00:53 Jordan (PM): target p95 under 250ms for chat, ideally p99 under 400ms. budget: we can't exceed $25k/month for model spend in year one for the pilot.
01:10 Priya: also we need audit logs and KMS for any PII-ish traces, and SSO via Okta.
01:17 Sara (Redwood): that's standard — we do SSO, KMS integrations, and audit logs in private or dedicated. hosted can also meet audit needs depending on retention choices.
01:28 Ethan: diving into unit economics — per-token pricing varies by model and hosting path. hosted has a published per-token rate, dedicated is lower per-token at scale but requires committed capacity, private has a platform + infra cost. key levers are: batching, prefix (KV) caching, and quantization.
01:47 Liam: can you unpack caching? we heard something about prefix cache and K V cache, sorry kayvee?
01:53 Ethan: yeah sorry — KV cache (key-value) holds the past hidden states for long-running conversations. with effective KV caching we can avoid re-computing prefixes which can drop per-request token work by up to 30-60% on long prompts. prefix caching is a lighter form — if many requests share the same system prompt you get hits there.
02:12 Priya: typical cache hit rate you'd expect?
02:15 Ethan: depends on product and prompt diversity. for support flows with templates, hit rates can be 40-70%. for free-form chat lower, maybe 10-25%. when we model economics we show scenarios: optimistic (50% hits), realistic (25%), low (10%).
02:30 Jordan: and batching harms latency, right?
02:33 Sara: batching amortizes GPU work but increases tail latency. Redwood offers continuous batching with latency-SLO-aware cutoff — you can cap batching window to e.g., 30ms for low-latency paths or allow 100–200ms windows for throughput-heavy flows. that's a control you can tune per route.
02:52 Olivia (Security): if we go dedicated or private how do you handle KMS and keys?
02:56 Maya: dedicated and private support customer-managed KMS; on hosted we offer envelope encryption with customer KMS in some enterprise tiers. we also provide audit logs and exportable traces for compliance.
03:09 Liam: any difference in per-token price when we use quantized models?
03:12 Ethan: model quantization reduces GPU memory and increases throughput on some kernels; person costs often drop because you can pack more concurrent sequences on the same GPU. For hosted, we surface separate SKUs/variants (e.g., q8fa / int8) with lower per-token pricing. For dedicated, you can run quantized variants and the unit cost improvement shows up as lower effective tokens/sec pricing.
03:34 Priya: what's the minimum commit for dedicated? we don't want to overcommit.
03:38 Maya: typical dedicated starter package is a 3–6 month reserved pool with predictable throughput. We can do flexible burst capacity on top for spikes. We also propose a pilot with limited reserved capacity to validate throughput — many customers start with a small commit and then expand.
03:54 Jordan: about fallback policies — if dedicated pool is saturated do you fallback to hosted or smaller models?
03:59 Ethan: yes, smart routing can fallback to hosted or to cheaper model variants with graceful degradation. you configure policies per route: priority regions, cost-first or latency-first, and automatic rollbacks.
04:15 Priya: can you run us through a quick worked example — 100k chat messages per day with average 20 tokens each, what would monthly burn look like under hosted vs dedicated?
04:24 Ethan: quick math — 100k * 20 = 2M tokens/day ~ 60M tokens/month. hosted per-token list price varies by model but say $0.000015/token for the base open model — that's ~$900/month. but that's naive: real numbers depend on generation vs prompt tokens, and we add top-ups for streaming and function calls. with caching and batching you can reduce effective tokens by 20–40% depending on flow. dedicated at scale with reserved capacity might bring the effective per-token down by 30–50% after amortizing GPU and infra.
04:56 Liam: those hosted per-token numbers sound low compared to what our infra shows; are we missing something?
05:00 Sara: yes, careful: list per-token is model-dependent. many customers run newer large models for quality and see higher per-token egress. also prompt tokens vs generated tokens and repetition increase burn. we usually run a short eval on your prompt corpus to get realistic burn estimates.
05:18 Priya: timeline: if we start pilot can we do a 2-week perf run and then 3-week validation?
05:23 Maya: yes, a typical pilot is 3–4 weeks: setup and onboarding (week 1), benchmark/validation (week 2), limited production/observation (week 3). we'll provide a pricing sheet and runbook.
05:36 Jordan: stakeholders — final signoff will be Priya + procurement + security. procurement expects a PO if we go dedicated.
05:42 Olivia: security question — do you have SOC 2 Type II and pen test reports we can share with our auditors?
05:48 Maya: yes, we'll share SOC 2 summary and pen test redacted reports. for private deployments we can do on-prem air-gapped installs but that adds infra cost.
05:59 Liam: curious about the impact of prompt engineering and templating on economics — any ballpark?
06:04 Ethan: prompt engineering can have big wins. removing unnecessary system tokens, truncating history before tokenizing, and templating common responses increases cache hits, reducing tokens and compute. some customers saw 15–30% token reduction from prompt tuning alone.
06:20 Priya: do you support per-route configs so we can set stricter low-latency rules for chat and higher throughput for async batch tasks?
06:25 Sara: yes — per-route policies are supported: SLO, batching window, cache behavior, model variant, fallback, and routing priority.
06:33 Jordan: FYI our infra team runs on GCP and we need private deployment options in us-central1.
06:38 Ethan: private/VPC is supported in that region — we have guidance for VPC peering and egress policies.
06:44 Olivia: any limitations on audit retention or log export?
06:47 Maya: retention is configurable; we can export logs to your SIEM or S3 for long-term retention. for hosted there are retention tiers; dedicated and private give more flexibility.
06:55 Priya: about burst spikes — we saw a 5x spike in promo periods; if we go dedicated will bursting to hosted add costs we can control?
07:03 Ethan: bursting to hosted is pay-as-you-go and will incur hosted per-token charges for overflow; you can set hard caps and failover behavior. another pattern is reserved baseline + burst buffer for promos.
07:15 Liam: for the benchmark, what do you need from us?
07:18 Ethan: we need a representative prompt corpus, p95/p99 latency SLO target, concurrency profile (RPS shape over hour/day), and an initial model preference (or we'll suggest based on quality).
07:30 Jordan: i can share that by monday.
07:32 Maya: perfect — we'll use that to create the burn model and pilot pricing.
07:36 Priya: how do you charge for embeddings or retrievers? separate per-embedding unit?
07:40 Sara: embeddings are billed separately per-embedding vector call — we provide batching and caching for retrievers as well, but embeddings have their own unit economics.
07:48 Olivia: encryption at rest — is customer key required for dedicated?
07:52 Maya: customer-managed KMS is optional but available. recommended for regulated PII.
07:56 Liam: any performance delta we should expect on private on-prem compared to hosted?
08:00 Ethan: depends on hardware. if you use identical GPU infra you'll see similar perf. our runtime picks kernels and compilers based on hardware; on-prem heterogeneity can cause variance, but our onboard profiling helps.
08:14 Priya: okay can we talk about pricing scenarios — conservative, realistic, aggressive?
08:18 Maya: yes. conservative assumes low caching (10%), high prompts (longer conversations), no batching for chat — that'll show higher per-token effective cost. realistic uses 25% caching, small batching windows for chat and larger for async, and some quantization where quality permits. aggressive assumes aggressive caching and batching for async pipelines and smaller model variants for low-risk flows.
08:42 Jordan: procurement will want to see worst-case run rate if caching is low.
08:46 Maya: we'll include worst-case in the pricing sheet and show sensitivity to cache hit rate and batching windows.
08:52 Olivia: about SLA — if you promise 99th pct latency targets what are credits?
08:56 Sara: enterprise SLA includes uptime and latency tiers with credits; details depend on the tier and hosting mode. we'll include a draft SLA in the docs.
09:06 Liam: can you share an example of the savings from moving hosted->dedicated at our scale (60M tokens/mo)?
09:10 Ethan: ballpark — if hosted effective is $0.00002/token (after quality selection) that's ~$1.2k/mo; dedicated amortization with a small reserved pool might cut that to $0.000012/token -> ~$720/mo plus reserved infra cost. exact numbers in the sheet.
09:30 Priya: those per-token figures seem lower than our current infra total cost; we pay a lot in ops and infra management. this could shift TCO meaningfully.
09:39 Maya: exactly — one of Redwood's selling points is reducing ops overhead and predictable unit economics.
09:44 Jordan: any data residency issues for EU customers? we have some customers in EU and APAC.
09:48 Sara: we have multi-region hosting and private deployments in target regions — residency is configurable, routing by policy ensures data stays in-region when required.
09:58 Olivia: will the pilot need a data processing agreement or special addendum?
10:02 Maya: we'll include the standard DPA and can add addenda for specific retention/regulatory needs.
10:07 Liam: one more technical — how do you measure effective tokens for caching math? do you instrument at request level?
10:12 Ethan: yes, we instrument tokens, cache hits/misses, and per-request latency — the console shows token breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and KV-cache hit rates.
10:21 Priya: okay lets recap next steps.
10:24 Maya: recap — we'll send: 1) pilot pricing and worst-case sensitivity sheet, 2) SOC2/KMS/SSO docs, 3) benchmark runbook and date options next week. Hyacinth will send: prompt corpus, RPS profile, compliance checklist.
10:41 Jordan: scheduled; we'll aim to get corpus by sunday and security details by monday.
10:45 Priya: we're onboard to try a pilot but need the worst-case numbers for procurement to sign off.
10:51 Maya: understood — we'll highlight worst-case and an optimistic breakout so procurement can see the delta.
10:56 Olivia: small note — we also want a non-technical one-pager explaining hosting differences for execs.
10:59 Maya: we'll include that.
11:02 Ethan: any final Qs?
11:05 Liam: none here. thanks.
11:07 Maya: great thanks everyone; we'll follow up with the packet tomorrow.
11:10 meeting end
